game.intro: The last page of the notes has vanished from the salon. Someone replaced it with an advert for steam Wi-Fi. Pass three trials to restore the archive.
game.text0: The envelope bears the publication year of the English translation with Ada’s notes. Which year unlocks the drawer?
game.hint0: The annotated translation appeared one year after the French article of 1842.
game.text1: Which label describes the real content of Note G?
game.hint1: Look for mathematics. Wi-Fi and TeaScript are inventions in this game.
game.text2: Using modern notation: B₀ = 1, B₁ = -1/2. The sum S = B₀ + 3 × B₁ = -1/2. What does the rule B₂ = -S / 3 give?
game.hint2: Negating the negative sum gives a positive half. Divide it by three.
game.finish: Archive rescued! Your reward: honorary Guardian of Note G. This is a game award.
game.solution: Answers: 1843; a procedure for Bernoulli numbers; 1/6. Discuss: which clues can a source verify? Which parts are fiction? The calculation uses a modern recurrence, not an exact transcription of Ada’s cards.
lesson.edit: You can edit the plan here before printing or downloading.
lesson.goal0: Students distinguish Ada’s notes, Babbage’s machine design and later legacy.
lesson.goal1: Students describe an algorithm as a precise procedure and repair one error.
lesson.goal2: Students check a claim against a source and distinguish evidence from an AI-generated image.
lesson.activity0: Ask: what could Ada really do in 1843?;Explore the Time Machine and locate 1843 and the explanation of Note G.;Put three events in order and match each to a person or source.;Each student shares one supported fact and one salon invention.
lesson.activity1: Ask students to dictate precise instructions for making tea.;In the punch-card workshop, observe state changes step by step.;Swap two steps, predict the outcome and repair the error.;Explain why the order of instructions changes the result.
lesson.activity2: Show a historical portrait and a labelled AI image from the gallery.;Open a claim and its source on Facts and Myths.;Write two sentences: a verified fact and a clearly labelled invention. Cite a source for the fact.;Ask: is a convincing image enough to establish a historical fact?
lesson.adapt0: Work in pairs. Use pictures and cards; fractions are optional. Students may answer orally.
lesson.adapt1: Students explain their reasoning and compare two claims. Provide a worked example for fractions.
lesson.adapt2: Students distinguish primary and secondary sources and discuss limits of evidence. Extension: compare the modern recurrence with Note G.
lesson.extension: For a longer lesson, add the detective game, source comparison and short presentations in pairs.

glossary.0text: A precise sequence of steps for solving a task.
glossary.1text: Babbage’s design for a programmable mechanical calculating machine.
glossary.2text: A card whose hole positions represent information.
glossary.3text: An original document from the period, such as Ada’s notes of 1843.
glossary.4text: Deliberately invented content, distinguished from history on this site.
glossary.5text: A rule that calculates a new value from values already known.
extra.0.q: What is a primary source for Ada’s work in 1843?
extra.0.options: Her published notes;An AI beach photo;Our fictional CV
extra.0.why: The original notes are a contemporary document. Modern inventions cannot replace them.
extra.1.q: If B₀ = 1 and B₁ = -1/2, what is B₀ + 3 × B₁?
extra.2.q: Which operation turns S = -1/2 into B₂ = 1/6?
extra.2.why: Negating the sum and dividing by three gives 1/6.
extra.3.q: What does our Bernoulli simulation show?
extra.3.options: A modern recurrence;A recording of the machine in 1843;An exact copy of all Ada’s cards
extra.3.why: The simulation explains the principle using a modern recurrence and notation.
extra.4.q: What does an AI image of Ada with a laptop prove?
extra.4.options: That she owned a laptop;Nothing about historical laptop ownership;That she invented the internet
extra.4.why: It is labelled fiction. A convincing appearance is not historical evidence.
extra.5.options: It is always arbitrary;It determines the computer’s colour;A later step may need an earlier result
extra.5.why: Step dependencies are part of an algorithm. A value must exist before it can be used.
